review.stories: In 1978 grandmaster Walter Browne bet he could win a queen against rook ending from the computer Belle within fifty moves. He couldn't. He studied, asked for a rematch and won the rook on exactly the fiftieth move.
Did you know that Philidor, of the Philidor position, was also a famous composer? His operas were hits in eighteenth-century Paris, and he played blindfold chess in public.

In 1858 Paul Morphy played a game in a box at the Paris Opera, during the performance, against the Duke of Brunswick and Count Isouard. He won with one beautiful sacrifice after another. It became known as the Opera Game.
The longest game ever played in a master tournament was Nikolić against Arsović, Belgrade 1989: 269 moves and more than twenty hours. It ended in a draw.

Capablanca learned chess at the age of four just by watching his father play. They say that in his first game he beat his own father. Years later he became world champion and kept saying: start with the endgames.
In 1997 IBM's computer Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov in a six-game match. It was the first time a world champion lost a match to a machine at tournament time controls.
The seven-piece endgame tablebases hold the perfect result of every position with up to seven pieces. The longest one needs 549 moves to mate: no human could play that from memory.
Marcel Duchamp, one of the most famous artists of the twentieth century, gave up painting to devote himself to chess. He played for France in several Olympiads and wrote a book on pawn endings.
In 1851, in London, Adolf Anderssen sacrificed both rooks, a bishop and his queen against Kieseritzky and mated with his minor pieces. The game became known as the Immortal Game.
In 1972, in Reykjavík, Bobby Fischer beat Boris Spassky in the most famous match in history, in the middle of the Cold War. Chess made the front page all over the world.

In 1921, Richard Réti published a study that looks impossible. The white king is far from the enemy pawn and far from his own. By walking along the diagonal, he threatens both at once and saves the draw. Sometimes the crooked path is the shortest.

In 1895, a Spanish priest living in Glasgow, Fernando Saavedra, looked at an ending everyone thought was a draw. He saw that making a queen allowed stalemate. He made a rook instead and won. A weak amateur entered history with a single move.

The Lucena position is named after Luis Ramírez de Lucena, but it is not in his 1497 book. The oldest record is by Alessandro Salvio, in 1634. The winning technique has a lovely name: building a bridge with the rook.

In 1777, Philidor showed how to draw with rook against rook and pawn. The defending rook sits on the third rank and holds the enemy king back. When the pawn advances, it drops back and checks from a distance. More than two centuries later, the recipe still works.

A king and two knights cannot force mate against a bare king. But if the defender has a pawn, sometimes they can. The Russian Alexei Troitsky studied this ending for years and published his analysis in 1937. The Troitsky line shows how far up the pawn can be blockaded.

Alexei Troitsky is seen as the father of the modern endgame study. He starved to death in 1942, during the siege of Leningrad. Many of his notes were lost in the war. What survived is still taught today.

In 1851, Josef Kling and Bernhard Horwitz published Chess Studies, a landmark of endgame theory. Kling had been a music teacher and later opened a London coffeehouse with chess rooms. Horwitz sometimes worked there as the house professional.

In 1851, Kling and Horwitz concluded that two bishops usually beat a knight. More than a century later, Ken Thompson's tablebases confirmed what they had found by hand. Good human analysis stands the test of time.
The fifty-move rule is old. Ruy López de Segura already had it in his 1561 book. In shatranj, the ancestor of chess, the limit was seventy moves. It exists so nobody can shuffle pieces forever.

Starting in 1928, FIDE made exceptions to the fifty-move rule for long endings. Then computers found endings that needed far more than 100 moves. The list of exceptions would never end. Around 1992, FIDE gave up and went back to fifty for everyone.

Luigi Centurini was a jurist in Genoa with a passion for endgames. In 1856 he published the rules for bishop and pawn against a bishop of the same color. He showed when the win is possible and when the defender holds. A lawyer's patience, applied to the board.

Josef Vančura died in 1921, barely past twenty. His analysis of rook and rook pawn against rook was only published in 1924. The idea: attack the pawn from the side, from far away. A young man left a defense that masters still use.

King, bishop and knight against a lone king shows up in about one game in six thousand. Because it is rare, many players never practice it. In 2013, Women's World Champion Anna Ushenina could not win it against Olga Girya, and the fifty-move rule gave a draw.

In 1965, the mathematician Richard Bellman proposed solving endgames backwards with a computer. That idea became endgame tablebases. By 2005, Eugene Nalimov and others had every position with up to six pieces, about 1.2 terabytes.

In 2013, Ronald de Man released the Syzygy tablebases, built for chess engines. They are much smaller than earlier ones. The complete seven-piece set came out in 2018. The engine reviewing your game likely relies on something like it.

Wilhelm Steinitz, born in Prague, beat Zukertort in 1886 and became the first official world champion. He taught players to gather small advantages before attacking. He changed chess, but never managed money well and died poor in 1900.

Emanuel Lasker was world champion for 27 years, from 1894 to 1921. No one has reigned longer. In his spare time he held a doctorate in mathematics and left an algebra theorem bearing his name. Einstein, his friend, called him one of the most interesting people he had met.

Alexander Alekhine lost the title to Max Euwe in 1935 and won it back in 1937. He died in Portugal in 1946, still champion, the only one to die with the crown. In 1933, in Chicago, he played 32 opponents blindfold at the same time.

Mikhail Botvinnik was an electrical engineer with a doctorate. After giving up the title, he started a chess school. Three of his students became world champions: Karpov, Kasparov and Kramnik. A good teacher multiplies.

Tigran Petrosian, world champion from 1963 to 1969, earned the nickname Iron Tigran: he was almost impossible to beat. His favorite weapon was an odd one. He would give a rook for a bishop or knight, not to attack, but to feel safer. Sometimes the player giving up material is the calm one.

The Karpov–Kasparov match began in September 1984 and simply would not end. After 48 games, 40 of them drawn, the FIDE president stopped it in February 1985, citing the players' health. Karpov led 5 to 3. In the new match, later in 1985, Kasparov won.

Henri Rinck, from Lyon, published around 1,670 endgame studies, and 58 of them took first prize in composing contests. He started in 1902 and never stopped. If you think you have seen every trick an ending holds, Rinck would politely disagree.

Hou Yifan became Women's World Champion in 2010, at 16, the youngest ever. Later she studied at Oxford as a Rhodes Scholar. Today she is also a university professor. Chess and study fit in the same life.

Vera Menchik was the first Women's World Champion, in 1927, and held the title until her death in 1944. Masters who lost to her jokingly joined the "Vera Menchik Club". Max Euwe, a future world champion, became a member twice.

In 1770, Wolfgang von Kempelen showed Empress Maria Theresa the Turk, a figure that seemed to play chess by itself. It beat almost everyone. The secret: a master hidden in the cabinet moved the pieces with levers and magnets. The most famous machine of the eighteenth century was, at heart, a cramped human.

In 2017, AlphaZero was given only the rules of chess and played itself for about nine hours. No one taught it openings or endings. Then it faced Stockfish 8 in 100 games: 28 wins, 72 draws and no losses. Nine hours. It took me rather longer.

The queen was not always strong. For centuries she moved just one square diagonally. In late fifteenth-century Spain she gained today's moves. Lucena's 1497 book already showed the novelty, which some called "madwoman's chess".

The pawn's two-square first move came in to speed up the game, and en passant came with it. Ruy López already described the capture in the sixteenth century. Italy was the last holdout: it only accepted it in 1880, ahead of the 1881 Milan tournament.

Chess clocks first came into real use at the London tournament of 1883, invented by Thomas Wilson of Manchester. More than a hundred years later, in 1988, Bobby Fischer filed a patent for the increment: a little extra time with every move.

Vasily Smyslov, world champion in 1957, was famous for his precise endgames. With Levenfish he wrote a classic book on rook endings. He was a baritone and only chose chess after failing an audition at the Bolshoi Theatre in 1950.

Henrique Mecking, known as Mequinho, was Brazilian champion at 13 and Brazil's first grandmaster. By 1978 he was world number 3. Then came myasthenia gravis, and many thought he would not survive. He did, spent the 1980s away from the board and returned to play in 1991. Stubbornness is a talent too.

Rafael Leitão won the World Youth Under-12 title in 1991 and the Under-18 in 1996. Then he became Brazilian champion seven times. Not satisfied, he also became a grandmaster in correspondence chess, where a single move can take days. The patience of someone who loves endgames, like you.

In May 2020, Brazil's Luis Paulo Supi beat Magnus Carlsen in an online blitz game in just 18 moves, giving up his own queen. Carlsen was streaming live and was stunned by the final move. The next year, Chess.com ranked that game first in its Immortal Game contest.

Krikor Mekhitarian, a Brazilian of Armenian family, learned to play at seven. As an adult, he earned all three grandmaster norms in just eight months, between 2009 and 2010. He has been Brazilian champion twice and now runs Chess.com's Portuguese content. Eight months, student. But years of study came first.

In 1512, the Portuguese Pedro Damiano, an apothecary from Odemira, published one of the first chess books in Rome. He believed the word for chess in Portuguese came from Xerxes; it doesn't. He also condemned 2...f6 as a bad move. The irony: today that bad defense is called the Damiano Defense.

In 1925, Richard Réti played 29 blindfold games at once in São Paulo, breaking the record of the time. On his way out, he left his briefcase behind and remarked on how poor his memory was. Twenty-nine boards in his head, no briefcase in his hand.

In 1947, in São Paulo, Miguel Najdorf played 45 blindfold games at once and won 39. He chased these records so the news would reach Europe and his family would learn he was alive. Sadly, they had already died in the concentration camps. Sometimes a record is a letter that never arrives.

The 1939 Chess Olympiad in Buenos Aires began its final stage on the very day World War II broke out. Many players never went back to Europe and stayed in South America, Najdorf among them. The ship that brought them, the Piriápolis, is remembered as chess's Noah's Ark.

Abhimanyu Mishra became a grandmaster at 12 years, 4 months and 25 days, in 2021. He broke a Karjakin record that had stood for 19 years. At 16, he beat world champion Gukesh in a classical game, the youngest ever to do so. And you're worried about your age...

In 2016, in Las Vegas, Timur Gareyev played 48 blindfold games at once, with a mask over his eyes, while pedaling an exercise bike. He scored 35 wins, 7 draws and only 6 losses. A world record. I'm happy if I remember where I left my glasses.

World Championship, Havana, 1892. Chigorin was a piece up against Steinitz and needed to win to stay alive in the match. He played 32.Bb4?? and allowed mate in two. More than a thousand people watched the Russian clutch his head in his hands. Match over. Before you move a piece, check what it defends.

2014 World Championship, game six. Carlsen played 26.Kd2?? and allowed a blow that would have given Anand two extra pawns. Anand missed it and quickly replied 26...a4?? Two champions, two mistakes in a row, and Carlsen won. Even at the top of the world, a second look costs nothing.

In 1970, in the USSR versus the Rest of the World match, Lajos Portisch had a winning position against Korchnoi. Without noticing, he repeated the position three times and gave away a draw. Many thought that half point decided the match, and Fischer was furious. Count your repetitions, student: a draw doesn't ask permission.

Bent Larsen was so confident that in 1970 he demanded to play first board for the Rest of the World, ahead of Fischer, and got his way. The next year they met in a match and Fischer won 6 to 0. Larsen blamed the heat. Confidence is great; preparation is better.

1978 World Championship, in the Philippines. Karpov was handed a blueberry yogurt during a game without asking for one. Korchnoi's team protested: it could be a coded message! There was also a hypnotist in the audience and chairs sent for X-rays. And you think your opponent is annoying.

Mikhail Tal had fragile health all his life and even lost a kidney. In May 1992, he left the hospital to play a blitz tournament in Moscow and still beat Kasparov. He died a month later. Some people play chess; Tal lived it.

Tigran Petrosian was hard of hearing and wore a hearing aid. It is said that against Gligorić he offered a draw and was turned down; seconds later Gligorić changed his mind and offered it back. Petrosian had switched his aid off, heard nothing, played on and won. Sometimes not hearing the noise helps.

Nona Gaprindashvili was women's world champion from 1962 to 1978. In 1977 she won the strong Lone Pine tournament against men, and in 1978 she became the first woman grandmaster. When a Netflix series said she had never faced men, she sued. They settled in 2022.

One night, Susan Polgár and her coach couldn't solve an endgame. They woke little Judit, carried her half asleep to the board, she showed them the solution and went back to bed. Endgames are like that: sometimes the answer is simple, it just needs fresh eyes.

Judit Polgár became a grandmaster at 15 years and 4 months, a month younger than Fischer had been for his record. In 2002, she beat Kasparov, then world number 1. Years earlier, Kasparov had said no woman could sustain a long fight. After that loss, he changed his mind. The board corrects a lot of people.

Magnus Carlsen reached a 2882 rating in 2014, the highest in FIDE history. Between 2018 and 2020 he played 125 elite classical games without a loss: 42 wins and 83 draws. Notice: most were draws. Not losing is an art too, and you learn it in the endgame.

Hikaru Nakamura became a grandmaster at 15, beating Fischer's American record by three months. Later he became famous in blitz and bullet, and one of the game's biggest streamers. In 2022 he beat Carlsen in the Speed Chess Championship final. That fast? Not even me in my youth.

When The Queen's Gambit premiered on Netflix in 2020, chess exploded. One American maker said its chess set sales rose more than a thousand percent, and Chess.com gained millions of new players. A show about a girl in an orphanage got the whole world studying openings.

In Ingmar Bergman's 1957 film The Seventh Seal, a knight returns from the Crusades and challenges Death to a game of chess to buy time. Bergman was inspired by a medieval painting in a church near Stockholm. Losing to Death is acceptable; to Stockfish, too.

In 1950, mathematician Claude Shannon estimated there are at least 10 to the power of 120 possible chess games. That's a 1 followed by 120 zeros. That's why nobody memorizes all of chess. We learn ideas, and endgames are full of them.

Many books say Gibaud lost to Lazard in just four moves in Paris, the shortest game ever between masters. But Gibaud denied ever losing a serious game in four moves, and historians don't accept that version. Even in chess, a good story isn't always a true one.

In 1999, Kasparov played a game over the internet against the World: more than 50,000 people from 75 countries voted on every move. The team's star was 15-year-old Irina Krush. It took 62 moves over four months, and Kasparov won in a very hard endgame. He called it the greatest game in history.

In 1970, aboard Soyuz 9, cosmonauts Nikolayev and Sevastyanov played chess against colleagues on Earth. It was the first documented game played in space, with pieces held by pegs, not magnets, so as not to disturb the ship. It ended in a draw. Even in orbit, a draw keeps its dignity.
tour.goal: Welcome. I am Viktor. I have spent my whole life in front of a chessboard, and I learned one thing: whoever masters the endgame masters chess. Let me show you around your new home.
tour.theme: First, make this home your own. Light or dark, and the color you like best. You can change everything later in Settings.
tour.board: Now the board. Choose the colors and pieces you like best. You can swap them whenever you wish.
tour.sound: One more choice: would you like to hear the pieces? Every move makes its sound, and I will warn you when the clock is running out. If you prefer silence, turn it off; you can change it later in Settings.
tour.voice: Hello! I'm Viktor. Before anything else: I can speak out loud, with your device's voice. Pick my voice; tap one to hear it. If you'd rather just read, choose "no voice". You can change it later in Settings.
tour.characterVoices: Your opponents also talk during the game. I've already picked a voice for each one; tap one to hear it and change it, or move on.
tour.rating: This number tells your story. It goes up and down, like every player's, even a world champion's. Do not fear it.
tour.journey: The Journey is a ladder. On every rung, a stronger opponent. At the very top, I will be waiting for you.
tour.endgames: This is where the endgames live: few pieces, nowhere to hide. Capablanca said this is where the study of chess should begin.
tour.opponents: Your opponents have personalities. Some tease, some tell stories. Listen, but do not get distracted: the board speaks louder.
tour.speedrun: Do you like a race against the clock? The speedrun measures how long you take to win a whole series. On to the next step.
tour.records: Every victory is kept. One day you will look back and smile at the road you travelled. You are doing well: just two more questions.
tour.level: Now tell me, honestly: where are you in your chess?
tour.level.test: Want to find out your level? Twenty questions, no clock, about 8 to 12 minutes. And at the end I will know where you should start.
tour.level.beginner: Just starting? What a joy. Then we begin at the beginning, together: how the pieces move, the first checkmates. I will be your teacher.
tour.goals: Last of all: what would you like to do here? Mark the paths you care about and they will stand out on the home screen. The rest stays there, one tap away.
tour.goals.placed: Done: now I know where you stand and what is missing. Last of all: what would you like to do here? The paths you mark stand out on the home screen.
school.welcome: This is my school. Every great player once stood exactly where you stand now. We will learn one step at a time.
school.welcomeBack: Good to see you back. Consistency beats talent.
Welcome back. Today's lesson is waiting for you.
The board is set. We can continue where we left off.
Every lesson you finish is one more stone in your foundation.
school.graduated: You graduated from my school. The Journey is yours now, and I am still up there, waiting for our reunion.
module.minorPieces: The rook and the minor pieces
pieces.rook.title: The rook
pieces.rook.summary: Straight lines, as far as it likes.
pieces.rook.intro: Let us start with the rook. It moves in straight lines, up, down and sideways, as many squares as it likes. Simple and powerful. A tip: when I mention a square, it shows up highlighted, like d4. Tap it and I will show it on the board.
pieces.rook.stars1: Take the rook to the stars. Tap the rook and then the target square, or drag it.
pieces.rook.stars1.done: Perfect. See how it crosses the whole board in a single move?
pieces.rook.block: An important rule: the rook cannot jump over pieces. The pawn on c6 blocks its way.
pieces.rook.stars2: Now collect the stars, going around the pawn.
pieces.rook.stars2.done: Well done. You already know how to move the rook.
pieces.bishop.title: The bishop
pieces.bishop.intro: The bishop moves along the diagonals, as many squares as it likes. It cannot jump over pieces either.
pieces.bishop.stars1: Take the bishop to the stars.
pieces.bishop.stars1.done: Great. Did you notice something curious about the squares it visited?
pieces.bishop.color: Each bishop lives on one colour only. This one, from c1, never leaves the dark squares; the one from f1, never the light ones. That is why we speak of the dark-squared and the light-squared bishop.
pieces.bishop.stars2: Now the light-squared bishop. Collect the stars.
pieces.bishop.stars2.done: Excellent. Bishops love long, open diagonals.
pieces.queen.title: The queen
pieces.queen.summary: Rook and bishop in one piece.
pieces.queen.intro: The queen is the strongest piece: she moves like the rook and like the bishop at the same time. Eight directions, as far as she likes.
pieces.queen.stars1: Collect the stars with the queen. Use straight lines and diagonals.
pieces.queen.stars1.done: Bravo. With a piece like this, checkmates will feel easy. But make no mistake: she needs help.
pieces.king.title: The king
pieces.king.summary: One square at a time, any direction.
pieces.king.intro: The king moves one square at a time, in any direction. He is the piece that can never be captured: if he falls, the game is over.
pieces.king.stars1: Walk the king to the stars, one square at a time.
pieces.king.stars1.done: Well done, no hurry and no mistakes.
pieces.king.active: A masters' secret: in the opening the king hides; in the endgame he becomes a warrior. An active king in the centre wins endgames. Never forget it.
pieces.knight.title: The knight
pieces.knight.summary: The L-shaped jump that clears everything.
pieces.knight.intro: The knight is the most unusual of all. He jumps in an L: two squares one way and one to the side. From here he reaches these eight squares.
pieces.knight.stars1: Take the knight to the stars. Think of the L before you move.
pieces.knight.stars1.done: That's it. Many players take a while to get used to the knight. You were quick.
pieces.knight.jump: And he has a superpower: he is the only piece that jumps over the others. Surrounded by pawns, he walks out as if nothing were there.
pieces.knight.stars2: One more route. This one takes a few jumps.
pieces.knight.stars2.done: Well done. The knight loves central squares, where he reaches the most.
pieces.pawn.title: The pawn and promotion
pieces.pawn.summary: The little one who can become a queen.
pieces.pawn.intro: The pawn moves forward, one square at a time. On each pawn's first move it may go two. And it never goes back.
pieces.pawn.double: Push the pawn two squares, using its first move.
pieces.pawn.double.hint: On its first move the pawn may go two squares: from e2 to e4.
pieces.pawn.capture: Careful: the pawn moves straight, but captures diagonally, one square forward.
pieces.pawn.take.hint: The pawn captures diagonally: from e4 to d5.
pieces.pawn.take.done: Right. The pawn is humble, but it bites.
pieces.pawn.promotion: Now the most beautiful part: a pawn that reaches the last rank turns into another piece. Almost always we choose a queen. Philidor called pawns the soul of chess.
pieces.pawn.promote: Promote the pawn. Choose the queen.
pieces.pawn.promote.hint: Push the pawn to e8 and choose the queen.
pieces.pawn.promote.done: A brand new queen! Remember this feeling: it drives every pawn endgame.
pieces.pawn.underpromotion: But the queen is not always the best choice. Here, with a queen on c8, the black king would not be in check and would have no move at all: that is stalemate, a draw, and we will talk about it soon. With a rook, the king still has a6, and you go on to win.
pieces.pawn.rook: Promote the pawn without stalemating the black king. Choose the rook.
pieces.pawn.rook.hint: Push the pawn to c8 and, when choosing the piece, tap the rook.
pieces.pawn.rook.done: A rook that wins is worth more than a queen that draws. Promoting to another piece has a name: underpromotion.
rules.captureProtect.title: Capture and protect
rules.captureProtect.summary: Take pieces, guard yours and give nothing away for free.
rules.captureProtect.capture: To capture is to move onto an enemy piece's square: it leaves the board. Each piece captures the way it moves; only the pawn is different, as you saw. Here the rook can capture the knight on d6.
rules.captureProtect.take: Your turn. Capture the black rook.
rules.captureProtect.take.hint: The bishop moves diagonally: from f1 it reaches a6.
rules.captureProtect.take.done: A free rook! Nobody was protecting that piece.
rules.captureProtect.protect: Now the knight is protected: the pawn on e6 guards d5. If the rook captures, the pawn captures the rook back. That is protection: one of your pieces looking after another.
rules.captureProtect.choose: The queen can capture two pieces. One is protected, the other is alone. Which one do you take?
rules.captureProtect.choose.hint: The knight on d5 is protected by the pawn on e6. The bishop on a4 is not.
rules.captureProtect.choose.done: Yes. The bishop was alone, and it is check as a bonus. Taking the knight would have cost the queen.
rules.captureProtect.defend: The black rook attacks your knight, and nothing protects it. Protect the knight with a pawn.
rules.captureProtect.defend.hint: A pawn protects the squares diagonally in front of it. Which pawn can guard d4?
rules.captureProtect.defend.done: There. If the rook captures, the pawn captures back, and Black loses a rook for a knight.
pieces.check.title: Check and checkmate
pieces.check.summary: Attack the king and leave no escape.
pieces.check.check: When a piece attacks the king, that is check. The king must get out of check on the very next move.
pieces.check.mate: And when the king is in check and has no way out, that is checkmate. Game over. Look: the rook attacks, and his own pawns lock the king in.
pieces.check.mate1: Your turn. Checkmate in one move.
pieces.check.mate1.hint: The black king is boxed in by his own pawns. Attack the back rank.
pieces.check.mate1.done: Checkmate! The famous back-rank mate. Many games between masters ended this way.
pieces.check.mate2: Now with the queen. Find the mate.
pieces.check.mate2.hint: Your king already covers the escape squares. The queen just needs the right check.
pieces.check.mate2.done: Beautiful. King and queen working together.
pieces.check.mate3: One more. The rook does the work, the king helps.
pieces.check.mate3.hint: Your king takes away the squares on the seventh rank. Use the rook on the last one.
pieces.check.mate3.done: Exactly. You will draw this picture many times.
rules.outOfCheck.title: Getting out of check
rules.outOfCheck.summary: Run, block or capture: the three ways out.
rules.outOfCheck.three: Check cannot be ignored: the attacked king must get out of check on that very move. There are three ways: run with the king, put a piece in the way, or capture the piece giving check.
rules.outOfCheck.run: Your king is in check and alone. Run to a safe square.
rules.outOfCheck.run.hint: The rook attacks the whole e-file. Get off it.
rules.outOfCheck.run.done: Safe. Running is the simplest way out, but it is not always there.
rules.outOfCheck.block: Now the king has nowhere to run. Put a piece in the rook's way.
rules.outOfCheck.block.hint: The bishop on d3 reaches f1, between the rook and the king.
rules.outOfCheck.block.done: That is blocking the check. The bishop became a shield.
rules.outOfCheck.capture: And the third way out: capture the piece giving check.
rules.outOfCheck.capture.hint: Your rook on a1 sees the black rook on e1.
rules.outOfCheck.capture.done: Captured! Sometimes the best defence is to remove the attacker.
rules.outOfCheck.none: And when none of the three works? The king cannot run, nothing can block, nobody can capture. That is checkmate. So before giving check, look at the enemy king's three ways out.
rules.castling.title: Castling
rules.castling.summary: The king gets safe and the rook joins the game, in one move. And when you cannot castle.
rules.castling.intro: Castling is the only move in which two pieces move together. The king goes two squares towards a rook, and the rook jumps over to its other side. King safe and rook in play.
rules.castling.short: Castle kingside: take the king from e1 to g1.
rules.castling.short.hint: Tap the king and then g1. The rook comes to f1 by itself.
rules.castling.short.done: Kingside castling. The king sits behind its pawns, well guarded.
rules.castling.long: Now castle queenside. The king also goes two squares, to c1.
rules.castling.long.hint: Take the king from e1 to c1. The rook on a1 jumps to d1.
rules.castling.long.done: Queenside castling. And the rook already lands on a central file.
rules.castling.rules: But there are rules. You cannot castle if the king or that rook has already moved, if there is a piece between them, if the king is in check, or if it passes through or lands on an attacked square. Here the bishop guards f1, and the king cannot pass through it.
rules.castling.cannot: The black bishop guards f1. Castle on the side where it is allowed.
rules.castling.cannot.hint: The king cannot pass through f1, attacked by the bishop. On the other side, the way is clear.
rules.castling.cannot.done: Exactly. Before castling, look at the squares the king passes through.
rules.castling.moved: One last rule: once the king has moved, even if it goes back to e1, it has lost castling for good. The same goes for a rook: the one that moved can no longer castle.
pieces.stalemate.title: Beware of stalemate
pieces.stalemate.summary: No check and no moves: a draw.
pieces.stalemate.stalemate: Look carefully. It is Black's move, the king is not in check, but he has nowhere to go. That is stalemate, and stalemate is a draw. I have seen many won games thrown away like this.
pieces.stalemate.avoid: Give checkmate, but careful: one careless queen move stalemates the king.
pieces.stalemate.avoid.hint: Before moving, ask: after my move, is the king in check? If not, and he has no squares, it is stalemate.
pieces.stalemate.avoid.done: Yes! Mate, not stalemate. Always leave the king a square, or give check.
pieces.stalemate.avoid2: Another one. Find the mate without stalemating.
pieces.stalemate.avoid2.hint: The queen must give check. Your king on g6 already guards the escape squares.
pieces.stalemate.avoid2.done: Perfect. You already think like an endgame player.
pieces.stalemate.defense: Now turn the board around. When you are losing, stalemate is a lifeline. Here Black has only the king, it is Black's move, there is no check and no move: a draw. King in the corner, in front of the rook pawn: the classic defence.
pieces.stalemate.save: You are Black, with only your king. Pick the right square and the pawn will not get through.
pieces.stalemate.save.hint: Go in front of the pawn, towards the a8 corner. Towards the centre, the white king pushes you out of the way.
pieces.stalemate.save.done: Yes. In the corner nobody can drive your king out: if White squeezes too hard, it is stalemate. Half a point saved.
rules.draws.title: Draws
rules.draws.summary: Insufficient material, repetition and fifty moves: when nobody wins.
rules.draws.insufficient: Stalemate is not the only draw. King and bishop against king: no mate is possible. That is insufficient material, and the game is drawn on the spot. The same goes for king and knight, or just the two kings.
rules.draws.takeLast: You only have your king. Capture the last black pawn: with king and knight, Black cannot give mate.
rules.draws.takeLast.hint: The pawn on d5 is next to your king, and nothing protects it.
rules.draws.takeLast.done: A draw! King and knight cannot mate on their own. Remember that when you are losing.
rules.draws.repetition: If the same position appears three times, it is a draw by repetition. The most common way is perpetual check: one side gives check after check, and the king cannot escape them. Here Black has much more material, but you have the queen.
rules.draws.perpetual: Keep giving check. Start with the queen on e8.
rules.draws.perpetual.hint: The queen goes back and forth between e8 and h5, always giving check.
rules.draws.perpetual.done: The position repeated. One more round and it appears for the third time: a draw. With less material, you saved the game.
rules.draws.fifty: And the fifty-move rule: if both sides make fifty moves each with no capture and no pawn move, it is a draw. So in the mates you are about to learn, do not dawdle: have a plan.
mates.twoRooks.title: Two-rook mate
mates.twoRooks.summary: The ladder: one rook fences, the other checks.
mates.twoRooks.wall: Our first real checkmate. Look: the rook on a4 builds a wall. The black king cannot cross to the fourth rank.
mates.twoRooks.ladder: The other rook checks on the king's rank. He has to climb. Then the first rook climbs and checks, and so on, like a ladder. We call it the ladder mate.
mates.twoRooks.climb: Let us climb the ladder together. Give the first check with the rook on b1.
mates.twoRooks.climb.hint: Alternate the rooks: the lower one climbs to the rank above the king and gives check.
mates.twoRooks.climb.done: Checkmate! The king reached the edge and had nowhere left to run.
mates.twoRooks.far: One warning: if the king comes close to your rooks, he attacks one of them. When that happens, move the rook to the far side of the board, on the same rank.
mates.twoRooks.play: Now without a script. Mate with the two rooks. I will be watching.
mates.twoRooks.play.tips: One rook fences, the other checks.
If the king touches a rook, send it far away on the same rank.
No hurry. The ladder never fails.
mates.twoRooks.play.done: Bravo! This mate is yours forever.
mates.queen.title: Queen mate
mates.queen.summary: The knight's jump and the king coming to help.
mates.queen.alone: The queen alone cannot mate a king. With your king's help, she can. This is the final picture: the queen right next to the black king, protected by your king.
mates.queen.jump: The secret: put the queen a knight's jump away from the black king. She closes a box around him, without checking and without getting too close.
mates.queen.box: Shrink the box: bring the queen closer while keeping the black king locked in.
mates.queen.box.hint: Look for a square a knight's jump from the black king that makes the box smaller.
mates.queen.box.done: Right. The box got smaller and the king is still trapped.
mates.queen.trap: The king is already trapped on the edge. Now the queen waits and your king does the work. Bring the king.
mates.queen.trap.hint: Leave the queen alone: she already holds the black king. Bring your king closer.
mates.queen.trap.done: Exactly. The queen holds, the king approaches. Patience is technique.
mates.queen.stalemateTrap.hint: The queen checks on a square protected by your king. Careful: Qg6 is stalemate!
mates.queen.stalemateTrap.done: Mate! And no stalemate. You learned the most important lesson of this ending.
mates.queen.play1: Now play until mate. The black king is already near the edge.
mates.queen.play1.tips: Queen a knight's jump from the black king.
Before each queen move: does the black king still have a square?
With the king on the edge, bring your king.
mates.queen.play1.done: Well done. Now from the centre, which is harder.
mates.queen.play2: From the centre of the board. Push the king to the edge, bring your king and mate.
mates.queen.play2.tips: The queen fences, but never touches the king.
Your king must come close for the mate.
mates.queen.play2.done: Queen mate mastered. That is no small thing: it is the ending that shows up most in real games.
technique.opposition.title: The king's wall
technique.opposition.summary: Opposition: one king blocking the other.
technique.opposition.wall: The kings can never stand next to each other. These three squares between them are forbidden to both. Each king is a wall for the other.
technique.opposition.opposition: Kings face to face with one square between them: that is the opposition. Whoever must move has to give way. Whoever does not have to move holds the opposition.
technique.opposition.take: Take the opposition: put your king face to face with the black king, one square between them.
technique.opposition.take.hint: Walk the king up the same file until one square separates it from the black king.
technique.opposition.take.done: That's it. Now he must move, and he must give way.
technique.opposition.keyPawn: Now with a pawn. Your king must go in front of the pawn and gain ground. What is the move?
technique.opposition.keyPawn.hint: The king goes in front of the pawn, not behind it. Advance the king.
technique.opposition.keyPawn.done: Perfect. With the king in front, the pawn gets through. That is the law of pawn endgames.
technique.opposition.defend: Now as Black, defending. The white king wants to clear the way for the pawn. Take the opposition yourself and do not let it through.
technique.opposition.defend.hint: Put your king face to face with the white king, one square between them.
technique.opposition.defend.done: That's it. With the opposition, the white king is the one who must give way. Whoever holds the opposition is in charge, on either side.
technique.zugzwang.title: Zugzwang
technique.zugzwang.summary: When having to move is the problem.
technique.zugzwang.idea: Zugzwang is a German word: the compulsion to move. Sometimes every move makes your position worse, and still you must play. Here Black has only one move, and it lets the pawn queen.
technique.zugzwang.tempo: But beware, zugzwang can turn against you too. Here Black has no move at all, and he is not in check: that is stalemate, a draw.
technique.zugzwang.wait: The kings face each other, but a check now does nothing: the king escapes or takes the rook. Make a waiting move with the rook, without check, and leave the black king with no good option.
technique.zugzwang.wait.hint: Move the rook to f7: it takes away f8, and the king can only go into the corner.
technique.zugzwang.wait.done: That is zugzwang! He was forced into the corner, and mate followed.
technique.zugzwang.pawnWait: Now with pawns. A pawn move can be the waiting move that wins the opposition. Find it.
technique.zugzwang.pawnWait.hint: The kings stand face to face. Use a pawn to pass the move to the black king.
technique.zugzwang.pawnWait.done: Well done. Spare pawn moves are worth gold in endgames.
technique.rookCut.title: Cutting off with the rook
technique.rookCut.summary: The rook as a fence: the king cannot cross.
technique.rookCut.cut: A rook on a rank, or on a file, is a fence. The enemy king cannot cross it. That makes life much easier.
technique.rookCut.cut1: Cut off the black king: with the rook, stop him from coming down to the bottom of the board.
technique.rookCut.cut1.hint: Put the rook on a rank just below the black king.
technique.rookCut.cut1.done: There. Half the board is now forbidden to him.
technique.rookCut.file: We can also cut along a file. The king is kept on one side of the board.
technique.rookCut.cut2: Cut off the black king along a file, keeping him on the left side.
technique.rookCut.cut2.hint: Move the rook to a file next to the black king.
technique.rookCut.cut2.done: That's it. A well-placed fence is worth more than many checks.
technique.rookMate.title: Rook mate
technique.rookMate.summary: Cut-off, opposition and waiting: all together.
technique.rookMate.final: The rook mate always ends like this: the black king on the edge, your king facing him in opposition, and the rook checks along the edge.
technique.rookMate.mate1.hint: The kings are in opposition. Check on the back rank.
technique.rookMate.mate1.done: Mate. Simple when the kings face each other.
technique.rookMate.plan: The full plan: the rook cuts the king off, your king comes into opposition, the rook checks and pushes him back a rank. When you lack the opposition, make a waiting move.
technique.rookMate.waitMate: Here the kings are not in opposition. One rook move solves it: cut the file and the black king has no choice.
technique.rookMate.waitMate.hint: Move the rook to the e-file. The black king will have to go to c8, facing your king.
technique.rookMate.waitMate.done: Mate! The cut left the king no choice, and the opposition did the rest.
technique.rookMate.play1: Now play. The black king is already on the edge.
technique.rookMate.play1.tips: Look for the opposition, then check.
No opposition? Waiting move with the rook.
A rook far from the black king is safe.
technique.rookMate.play1.done: Well done. Now the whole way, from the centre.
technique.rookMate.play2: From the centre. Cut off, push, wait and mate. The most technical ending so far.
technique.rookMate.play2.tips: The rook cuts off, the king approaches.
Every check with opposition pushes the king back a rank.
Patience. Even grandmasters play this mate calmly.
technique.rookMate.play2.done: Magnificent! The rook mate proves you understand endgames.
rules.enPassant.title: En passant
rules.enPassant.summary: Capturing in passing: a pawn that jumps two squares can be caught.
rules.enPassant.idea: Remember that a pawn may move two squares on its first move? If it jumps two squares and lands next to an enemy pawn, that pawn may capture it as if it had moved only one. That is en passant, French for "in passing".
rules.enPassant.capture: The black pawn has just jumped from d7 to d5, next to yours. Capture en passant.
rules.enPassant.capture.hint: Your pawn goes diagonally to d6, the square the black pawn skipped, and captures it.
rules.enPassant.capture.done: En passant! The pawn on d5 leaves the board, even though yours went to d6.
rules.enPassant.now: Careful: it only works on the move right after the jump. If you play something else, you lose the right. And it is only pawn against pawn.
rules.enPassant.black: Now as Black. White pushed the pawn from c2 to c4. Capture en passant.
rules.enPassant.black.hint: Your pawn on d4 captures diagonally, going to c3.
rules.enPassant.black.done: Perfect. Now you know the most curious rule in chess.
pawns.kingPawn.title: King and pawn against king
pawns.kingPawn.summary: The king in front, clearing the way.
pawns.kingPawn.front: This is the most important ending in chess. The secret: the king goes in front of the pawn, clearing the way, never behind it.
pawns.kingPawn.key: For this pawn, d4, e4 and f4 are the key squares. If your king reaches one of them, the pawn queens no matter what the other king does.
pawns.kingPawn.step: Occupy a key square with the king.
pawns.kingPawn.step.hint: The king steps in front of the pawn, onto d4, e4 or f4.
pawns.kingPawn.step.done: Yes! With the king on a key square, the win is certain.
pawns.kingPawn.play: Now play until the pawn promotes. King in front, opposition when needed.
pawns.kingPawn.play.tips: King in front of the pawn.
Do not push the pawn too early.
pawns.kingPawn.play.done: Promoted! This ending has decided world titles.
pawns.square.title: The rule of the square
pawns.square.summary: Can the king catch the pawn? Draw a square.
pawns.square.square: A trick that saves calculation: draw a square from the pawn to its promotion square. If the king can step into the square, he catches the pawn.
pawns.square.catch: The black pawn is going to run. Step into the square with your king to catch it.
pawns.square.catch.hint: The square goes from a5 to e1. Bring the king inside it.
pawns.square.catch.done: Right. Inside the square, the king catches the pawn in time.
pawns.square.run: Now the other way round: the black king is outside your pawn's square. So just run!
pawns.square.race.hint: The black king cannot catch it. Push the pawn.
pawns.square.race.done: Exactly. When the king is outside the square, the pawn queens on its own.
pawns.rookPawn.title: Rook and pawn against king
pawns.rookPawn.summary: The rook protects, the pawn advances.
pawns.rookPawn.team: With the rook cutting off the black king, the pawn walks forward calmly. Bring your king along if you need to.
pawns.rookPawn.play: Promote the pawn. First cut the king off with the rook.
pawns.rookPawn.play.tips: Cut the black king off with the rook.
A protected pawn is a happy pawn.
Do not let the black king get in front of the pawn.
pawns.rookPawn.play.done: Well done. A new queen, and the mate is just technique.
pawns.rookTwoPawns.title: Rook and two pawns against king and pawn
pawns.rookTwoPawns.plan: You have much more material, but the black pawn also wants to queen. Plan: cut the king off with the rook, push your pawns together and keep an eye on the enemy pawn.
pawns.rookTwoPawns.play.tips: Pawns side by side protect each other.
The rook cuts off the black king.
If the black pawn runs, the rook catches it from behind.
pawns.rookTwoPawns.play.done: Excellent! You converted your advantage calmly, like a professional.
minor.rookBishop.title: Rook and bishop against king
minor.rookBishop.team: The bishop is a great helper: while the rook cuts ranks, he cuts diagonals. Learn to use the bishop on the long diagonals.
minor.rookBishop.mate: Find the mate with the bishop's help.
minor.rookBishop.mate.hint: The bishop guards one escape square. The rook checks on the back rank.
minor.rookBishop.mate.done: Mate! Rook and bishop, a fine pair.
minor.rookBishop.play.tips: The rook cuts off, the bishop helps.
minor.rookBishop.play.done: Well done. You knew how to use the bishop.
minor.rookKnight.title: Rook and knight against king
minor.rookKnight.summary: The knight takes squares up close.
minor.rookKnight.team: The knight works up close: he takes away squares the rook cannot reach.
minor.rookKnight.mate: Find the mate with the knight's help.
minor.rookKnight.mate.hint: The knight on f6 and your king already surround the black king. The rook gives the check.
minor.rookKnight.mate.done: Mate! The knight is sneaky, isn't he?
minor.rookKnight.play.tips: The rook cuts the king off.
A knight close to the black king takes away escape squares.
minor.rookKnight.play.done: Well done. The knight knows how to work in a team too.
minor.rookTwoBishops.title: Rook and two bishops against king
minor.rookTwoBishops.team: Two bishops cover the light squares and the dark ones. Together with the rook, the black king has nowhere to hide.
minor.rookTwoBishops.play: Give mate. Use the bishops to cut the king off.
minor.rookTwoBishops.play.tips: Bishops side by side make a wall.
The rook does not have to work alone.
minor.rookTwoBishops.play.done: Mate! With this much power, technique is what counts.
minor.rookTwoKnights.title: Rook and two knights against king
minor.rookTwoKnights.team: Two knights and a rook. Knights are slow, so bring them near the black king early.
minor.rookTwoKnights.play: Mate with rook and two knights.
minor.rookTwoKnights.play.tips: Knights near the centre reach more squares.
The rook cuts off, the knights close in.
minor.rookTwoKnights.play.done: Well done! You coordinated very different pieces.
minor.rookBishopKnight.title: Rook, bishop and knight against king
minor.rookBishopKnight.team: Rook, bishop and knight: each with its own way of moving. The secret is making them all work together.
minor.rookBishopKnight.play: Give mate with the whole team.
minor.rookBishopKnight.play.tips: Bishop on the long diagonals, knight near the king.
minor.twoRooksVsKnight.title: Two rooks against king and knight
minor.twoRooksVsKnight.defender: Now the black king has a helper: the knight. He will try to attack your rooks and give checks. Keep your rooks protected or far from the knight.
minor.twoRooksVsKnight.play: Win. Capture the knight if you can; if not, give mate.
minor.twoRooksVsKnight.play.tips: Rooks far from the knight, or protected.
Sometimes trading is the best defence.
minor.twoRooksVsKnight.play.done: Well done. You beat an opponent who was really defending.
graduation.twoBishops.title: Two-bishop mate
graduation.twoBishops.wall: The final exam. Two bishops side by side make a diagonal wall the king cannot cross.
graduation.twoBishops.corner: With two bishops, mate only happens in a corner. The plan: drive the king to the edge, then into a corner, with your king always helping.
graduation.twoBishops.mate: The black king is in the corner. Give mate.
graduation.twoBishops.mate.hint: The bishop on e5 covers b8; your king covers a7 and b7. The other bishop checks along the long diagonal.
graduation.twoBishops.mate.done: Mate! That is the picture you will be aiming for.
graduation.twoBishops.play1: Play until mate. The black king is already near the corner.
graduation.twoBishops.play1.tips: Your king close to the black king.
Watch out for stalemate in the corner.
graduation.twoBishops.play1.done: Well done. Now the real exam.
graduation.twoBishops.play2: From the centre of the board. This is the final exam of my school. Use everything you have learned.
graduation.twoBishops.play2.tips: A wall of bishops, the king helping.
Push to the edge, then into the corner.
No hurry. I believe in you.
A waiting move, when you need one.
graduation.twoBishops.play2.done: You did it. Mate with two bishops.
coach.praise: That's right. You are doing very well.
coach.wrong: Not that one. Think a little more.
Calm. Everyone makes mistakes, even grandmasters.
coach.hint: Look at the arrow. Why this move?
This is the move I would play.
Look at the arrow and try to understand the idea.
coach.exerciseStart: Your move. Find the best plan.
Think it through before you touch a piece.
Your turn. What does this position ask for?
coach.keepGoing: You are on the right track.
coach.stalemate: Stalemate! The king was not in check and had nowhere to go. That is a draw. Let us try again, and this time leave him a square.
You stalemated the king. It happens to everyone once. Only once, agreed? Again.
coach.draw: It ended in a draw. The win slipped away, but the lesson stays. Try again.
A draw. Breathe, and let us go again.
coach.lost: You were mated. It happens. Again, calmly.
coach.retry: Once more. Now you know the way.
coach.partDone: Part done. Each one makes the next easier.
Good. One more piece of the technique in place.
Part complete. Rest your head for a moment, then go on.
coach.lessonDone: Lesson complete. I am proud of you.
Well done. One more step on your road.
You learn quickly. Shall we go to the next one?
That is real chess. Keep it up.
Every master once took this very lesson. Now you have too.
coach.graduation: You graduated. Remember the first lesson, when the rook still crawled across the board? Look how far you have come. Now climb the Journey rung by rung. At the top, I will be waiting for you, no longer as your teacher, but as your opponent.
journey.reunion: You came back. I remember your first day at school, when the rook still moved slowly. Today I am the last rung between you and the top. Come, my student: show me everything you learned. Being surpassed by a student is a teacher's greatest honour.
endgames.welcome: These are the endgame lessons. Each one goes deep into an endgame every player must master: the lesson, the exercises with stars and, at the end, the real endgame. Choose where to begin.
endgames.welcomeBack: Good to see you again. Endgames are in no hurry, but they have a method.
You are back. Every star you earn is a position you will never lose again.
The board is set. Let us continue where we stopped.
endgames.allPassed: You have passed every endgame lesson. The knowledge is yours now: take it to your games.
endgames.lesson.intro: The lesson comes in short parts. In each one you think alone first, then I show you and you practice. Start with Part 1.
endgames.lesson.middle: Good to see you back. Go on with the highlighted part: it is where you stopped.
endgames.lesson.test: Parts done. Now the final test, without my help. Once your score passes the minimum, I unlock the real endgame.
endgames.lesson.passed: Passed. Now all that is left is to prove it against a flesh-and-blood opponent: or a silicon one.
endgames.lesson.failed: Not this time. Reread the lesson if you like and redo the exercises: the second time is usually much better.
endgames.lesson.lessonLeft: You reached the score in the exercises. Now finish the lesson parts to complete the lesson and unlock the real endgame.
notation.coordinates.title: Coordinates
notation.coordinates.summary: Every square has a name: the file letter and the rank number.
notation.coordinates.intro: Every player speaks the same language: each square has a name. Files are letters, a to h, left to right. Ranks are numbers, 1 to 8, bottom to top. The bottom left corner is a1.
notation.coordinates.find: Let us practice. I say the square, you tap it. Letter first, then number.
notation.coordinates.find.hint: Find the file by the letter on the bottom edge and go up to the rank number.
notation.coordinates.find.done: Perfect. You can read the board.
notation.coordinates.blind: Now without the letters and numbers on the edge. Remember: a1 is bottom left.
notation.coordinates.blind.hint: Count the files from the left (a, b, c...) and the ranks from the bottom.
notation.coordinates.blind.done: No help at all. Well done!
notation.coordinates.end: From now on, when I mention a square like e4 or d5, you will know where it is. And you can tap it in what I say to see it on the board.
notation.moves.title: Naming a move
notation.moves.summary: The piece letter, the destination square, the capture and the check.
notation.moves.letters: A move is written with the piece letter and the square it goes to. K is the king, Q the queen, R the rook, B the bishop and N the knight. The pawn has no letter. Rd7 means: the rook goes to d7.
notation.moves.rook.hint: R is the rook. Take the rook to d7.
notation.moves.capture: When a piece captures, an x goes in the middle. Play Rxe5: the rook captures on e5.
notation.moves.capture.hint: The rook goes to e5 and takes the pawn.
notation.moves.capture.done: Rxe5. The rook took the pawn.
notation.moves.check: A check gets a + at the end. Play Qh5+: the queen goes to h5 and gives check.
notation.moves.check.hint: Q is the queen. She goes to h5 along the diagonal.
notation.read.title: Reading a move
notation.read.summary: Knight, pawn and castling: the written move becomes a move on the board.
notation.read.knight: Now you read it. Play Nf3.
notation.read.knight.hint: N is the knight. Look for f3.
notation.read.knight.done: Nf3, one of the most common moves in chess.
notation.read.pawn: The pawn has no letter: just the square. Play e4.
notation.read.pawn.hint: Push the e2 pawn two squares, to e4.
notation.read.pawn.done: e4. The most famous move in the world.
notation.read.castle: Kingside castling is written O-O. Play O-O: the king moves two squares towards the rook.
notation.read.castle.hint: Take the king from e1 to g1; the rook jumps to f1 by itself.
notation.read.end: Done: you can read and write moves. It is the language I use in the lessons, and with it you can play blindfold, saying or typing your moves.
rules.pieceValue.title: The value of the pieces
rules.pieceValue.summary: Pawn 1, knight and bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9: the arithmetic of trades.
rules.pieceValue.values: Every piece has a value, counted in pawns. A pawn is worth 1. Knight and bishop, 3. Rook, 5. Queen, 9. The king has no price: without him, there is no game.
rules.pieceValue.bigger: Your pawn can capture two pieces. Which one is worth more?
rules.pieceValue.bigger.hint: A knight is worth 3, a rook is worth 5. Capture the rook.
rules.pieceValue.bigger.done: Yes: 5 points in one go. Counting makes a difference.
rules.pieceValue.trade: A trade is capturing and being captured back. If the bishop takes the knight and the pawn takes the bishop, that was 3 for 3: a fair trade. But giving a rook for a knight loses 2 points.
rules.pieceValue.goodTrade: The black rook is protected by the pawn. You can capture it with the queen or with the knight. Which capture is a good deal?
rules.pieceValue.goodTrade.hint: If the pawn captures back, how much do you lose in each case? A queen is worth 9, a knight 3.
rules.pieceValue.goodTrade.done: Knight for rook: you gave 3 and won 5. With the queen it would have been 9 for 5.
rules.pieceValue.count: Before capturing, count: how much do I win, how much do I lose. With that sum, you stop giving pieces away and start winning your opponent's.
tricks.scholarsMate.title: Scholar's mate
tricks.scholarsMate.summary: Queen and bishop against the weak f7 square: beginners' most famous checkmate.
tricks.scholarsMate.weak: At the start of the game, f7 is Black's weak spot: only the king defends it. Play against beginners and you will see it attacked a lot. Let us learn to attack it, and then to defend it.
tricks.scholarsMate.attack: You play White. Open the way with e4, aim the bishop at f7 with Bc4, bring the queen to h5 and, if Black is careless, take on f7.
tricks.scholarsMate.attack.hint: Bishop and queen aim together at the same square: f7.
tricks.scholarsMate.attack.done: Scholar's mate! Queen on f7, protected by the bishop. The king has nowhere to go.
tricks.scholarsMate.why: Why it is mate: the queen checks on f7, the c4 bishop protects her, and the black king is boxed in by its own pieces. Two attackers against one defender.
tricks.scholarsMate.warning: A teacher's word: against someone who defends well, bringing the queen out early costs dearly, because she becomes a target while your other pieces sit still. Use the trick, but learn the real game.
tricks.defendScholar.title: Defending the scholar's mate
tricks.defendScholar.summary: As Black: guard f7 calmly and gain time by attacking the queen.
tricks.defendScholar.threat: Now you are on the other side. White threatens Qxf7, mate. Queen and bishop both aim at f7. Before anything else: what does White want?
tricks.defendScholar.guard: Defend f7. The best idea: g6, which defends and attacks the queen. Then, if the queen goes back to f3 aiming at f7 again, block the way with the knight.
tricks.defendScholar.guard.hint: Threaten the queen or guard f7. Then put the knight between the queen and f7.
tricks.defendScholar.guard.done: Perfect. f7 is safe and your knight is out. White's queen has moved three times and won nothing.
tricks.defendScholar.chase: That is the secret against the scholar's mate: do not panic. Defend with moves that develop pieces and attack the queen. Every time she runs, you gain a tempo.
tricks.foolsMate.title: Fool's mate
tricks.foolsMate.summary: The fastest checkmate in chess: what happens when the king is left unprotected.
tricks.foolsMate.intro: White played f3, a move that opens the diagonal to its own king. You are Black. If White blunders again with g4, your queen comes to h4 with mate.
tricks.foolsMate.punish: Open the way for your queen and wait for the second mistake. When the diagonal to the king is open, deliver mate.
tricks.foolsMate.punish.hint: First free the queen by moving the king's pawn. Then the queen goes to h4.
tricks.foolsMate.punish.done: Fool's mate! In two moves. The diagonal from h4 to e1 was open, and nothing can block it.
tricks.foolsMate.lesson: The lesson works both ways: don't push the f and g pawns early without a reason. They are the king's shield.
tactics.matePatterns.title: Checkmate patterns
tactics.matePatterns.summary: Back rank, smothered, Arabian and supported queen: pictures that repeat.
tactics.matePatterns.intro: Mates repeat themselves. Masters do not calculate everything: they recognise the picture. I will show you four pictures that come up all the time.
tactics.matePatterns.backRank: The back-rank mate. The black king is trapped behind his own pawns. Give mate.
tactics.matePatterns.backRank.hint: The last rank is undefended. Take the rook there.
tactics.matePatterns.backRank.done: Back rank! That is why masters open a window for the king, pushing one of the pawns in front of him.
tactics.matePatterns.smothered: The smothered mate: the king hemmed in by his own pieces, and a knight gives the check nobody can block.
tactics.matePatterns.smothered.hint: The knight jumps over everything. Find the square from which it attacks h8.
tactics.matePatterns.smothered.done: Smothered! The king had no free square, and a knight check cannot be blocked.
tactics.matePatterns.arabian: The Arabian mate: rook and knight together. The knight protects the rook and guards an escape square.
tactics.matePatterns.arabian.hint: Take the rook next to the king, onto a square the knight protects.
tactics.matePatterns.arabian.done: Arabian mate! The rook gives check, the knight holds the rest.
tactics.matePatterns.supported: And the supported queen: the queen gives check right next to the king, protected by another piece, and he cannot take her.
tactics.matePatterns.supported.hint: The bishop on d3 aims at h7. The queen captures there, protected.
tactics.matePatterns.supported.done: Mate! Queen next to the king and protected: one of the most common pictures of all.
tactics.matePatterns.end: Back rank, smothered, Arabian and supported queen. Keep the pictures and look for them in your games, on both sides: to give them and to avoid them.
tricks.principles.title: How to start a game
tricks.principles.summary: Center, pieces in play and a safe king: the three opening rules.
tricks.principles.center: Three rules to start well. First: take the center, the squares d4, e4, d5 and e5. A piece in the center watches more squares.
tricks.principles.develop: Now play. A pawn in the center, then the knight, the bishop and finally castling: the king goes to the corner, safe.
tricks.principles.develop.hint: A good order: center pawn, knight to f3, bishop out, castle.
tricks.principles.develop.done: That is a healthy opening: center, two pieces in play and the king safe. In four moves.
tricks.principles.rules: Summary: take the center, develop the knights and bishops, castle early. And don't move the same piece twice without a reason.
tricks.principles.online: Now comes the fun part: playing against people. Create a free account on Lichess, at lichess.org, and use these tricks in your first games, including defending against them. Then come back here: endgames are what win games.
